sources.title: PhyAI: Real-Time Physical AI at the Edge, Scalable Rollouts in the Cloud

sectionsRead: Sections 3.1–3.4 (task, control-time Roofline, deployment and batching)
Sections 5.1–5.5 (measurement settings, latency, phase/batch analysis and RL)
Sections 6.1–6.5 and 7.1–7.3 (future work, discussion and conclusion)
omissions: Text extraction does not reconstruct figure images; inspect the retained PDF for figures and equation/table layout.
Separate supplemental material availability has not been fully verified.
The figure-extraction limitation was addressed by inspecting original PDF pages and six faithful crops. All eight supplied text chunks were read individually, including references and Appendices A–E.

Identity: the supplied title and 26-author list match the catalog. The inspected artifact is arXiv:2608.03682v3, dated 14 August 2026. The catalog URL is unversioned; earlier revisions were not supplied, and their differences or original submission date cannot be established.
Code, benchmark harnesses, archived runs and separate supplements were not inspected; no experiments were reproduced. Availability statements about these resources remain author claims.

synopsis: PhyAI is a shared inference runtime for existing vision-language-action and world-action policies. Model adapters retain policy semantics while runners, graph replay, fused kernels and parallel services accelerate execution. The experiments establish model-runner speedups and model-dependent batching behavior; appendices add simulation success checks. Control-rate ceilings and RL speedup projections require separate interpretation from measured latency.

problem.text: A checkpoint may pass through evaluation, RL rollout, edge serving and onboard execution, each with a separate implementation. PhyAI addresses this duplication while accommodating reusable VLA conditions and evolving WAM latents. Its design target is a consistent inference path across deployment settings.

contributions.text: A scheduler–runner–Layers ownership hierarchy shares execution services while preserving architecture-specific preprocessing, cache validity, solver order and action conversion.
The control-time Roofline relates inference speed to the next action handoff; phase profiles explain why batching and within-request parallelism suit different workloads.

inputs: Recent camera observations, language instruction and robot state
Existing policy checkpoint and model-specific execution configuration
outputs: Decoded action chunk for controller handoff
For Cosmos3, evolving video/action states and optional decoded video

steps.name: Separate request state from computation
steps.detail: The scheduler assigns requests and device groups without owning model tensors. Stateful runners manage KV caches, buffers, graph buckets, solver updates and action assembly. Stateless modeling modules express computation through Layers; the operator selector chooses kernels using shape, dtype, accelerator and execution configuration.

steps.name: Reuse only valid conditions
steps.detail: For standard π0.5, compute the fixed vision-language prefix once across ten Euler steps. Cache its KV tensors and attention metadata, precompute timestep/modulation tables, and capture the stable loop in a CUDA Graph. New observations or conditions invalidate that prefix. Fused projections, activations and normalization reduce launches and intermediate traffic.

steps.name: Distribute the appropriate unit of work
steps.detail: π0.5 data-parallel workers process independent requests. Cosmos3 keeps video and action tokens in one GEN sequence, shards transformer computation within each guidance branch, then exchanges conditional/unconditional velocities between matching TP ranks. Each rank applies guidance and advances local video/action UniPC states. Optional tiled VAE decoding follows the last update.

training.text: PhyAI introduces no policy-learning objective or distillation procedure. It executes existing checkpoints; offline round-to-nearest quantization prepares optional low-precision artifacts. The reported phase/batch profiles use BF16. RLinf retains environment orchestration and policy optimization; PhyAI targets its inference-backend boundary.

inference.text: A request ends when its complete action chunk is ready. Controller handoff and physical execution are separate stages, and the executed horizon can be shorter than the predicted horizon. Skipping Cosmos3 video decoding still retains joint video/action latent evolution during generation.

equations.explanation: Environment time is the interval until the next policy decision; inference time produces one chunk. Control time either adds these stages or ideally overlaps them. X below one is inference-bound; above one is environment-bound. The plotted roof excludes observation, transport, queueing and handoff overhead.
B is synchronized batch size, T_sync is time until all outputs are ready, Q is completed requests per unit time, and T_amort is amortized cost. Every request still waits for the full batch.
Cosmos3 combines unconditional and conditional video/action velocities with guidance scale γ. This scale is independent of the number of parallel CFG branches.

results.setting: Eight H20 GPUs; CFG parallel degree 2, TP degree 4; model-runner latency.
results.interpretation: A matched-hardware runtime improvement; no matched FlashRT result is available for this configuration.

results.setting: Table 5 pairs π0, π0.5, GR00T N1.7 and MiniCPM-Robot with their listed devices.
results.comparison: π0.5 official: 52.076 ms. Range endpoints are GR00T/Thor and MiniCPM-Robot/H100.
results.interpretation: Specialized runtimes sometimes win; Figure 1 includes explicitly marked FP8 comparisons.

results.setting: Hopper-series GPU; BF16, three cameras, 50 actions, ten Euler steps, CUDA Graphs.
results.interpretation: The 10.00 ms amortized cost at batch 32 is not request latency. Expert time share falls from 57.2% to 13.5%.

results.setting: Hopper-series GPU; eager BF16, four steps, guidance scale 3.0, 32 actions, 33 frames at 480 × 832; optional video decode excluded.
results.interpretation: Only 14.3% throughput gain; generation already uses compute heavily. This is separate from the eight-H20 comparison.

results.setting: RTX 5090, BF16; two 256 × 256 views, action shape 40 × 132, four flow steps, CUDA Graphs.
results.value: Batch 32: 138.8 samples/s; batch 8 reaches 92.2% of that.
results.interpretation: Backbone becomes dominant from batch four; further batching increasingly raises synchronized wait.

results.setting: H20, BF16, CUDA Graph path; add two fused kernels.
results.interpretation: A local combined-kernel ablation, without separate attribution to each kernel.

results.setting: A40; same checkpoint, 50 initial states/task, seeds 42–91, batch 1, first eight actions executed, 720-step cap.
results.interpretation: Three more successes, or 0.6 percentage points; no significance test or uncertainty is reported.

results.task: π0.5 success across four LIBERO suites
results.setting: 500 episodes per suite; synchronous ten-action chunks, BF16 and CUDA Graphs.
results.interpretation: Author-reported simulation results; inference means are 36.10–36.33 ms, with GPU model unspecified in Appendix C.

results.task: π0 success on LIBERO spatial and object
results.setting: Batch 1; ten episodes/task; BF16; execute each 50-action chunk before querying again.
results.interpretation: Different policy, horizon and episode count prevent direct comparison with Appendix C.

results.setting: LIBERO-10 baseline on four A800 80 GB GPUs without NVLink; 32 environments, four denoising steps.
results.metric: Mean predict speedup and projected step time
results.value: Measured predict speedup: 2.55×. Projected step: 863.2 s, 9.7% lower, 1.11× faster.
results.comparison: Baseline step: 955.8 s; maximum-rank predict time: 152.4 s.
results.interpretation: Amdahl projection holds non-predict work fixed, assumes accelerated calls remain critical and adds no integration overhead; not measured end-to-end.

limitations.text: Internal v3 differences remain unresolved: the introduction instead describes an eight-A100 rollout simulation projecting 26.5% lower latency and 1.36× throughput; Section 5.4 uses four A800 GPUs. Section 6.3 still calls usable RLinf integration future work. These accounts must not be merged.

Section 5.5 excludes closed-loop quality and tail latency from its summary, although Appendices A/C/E report simulation success and Figure 6 plots runner P99. The narrower reading is warranted: full deployment tail latency, physical-robot quality and integrated RL gains remain unestablished.

Logical arithmetic intensity uses modeled tensor traffic, not measured DRAM transfers. Phase profiles diagnose batch behavior without isolating all optimizations or measuring distributed scaling. The Hopper-series device is unnamed.

reproduction.text: Match checkpoint, precision, camera order, solver steps and executed horizon before timing. Profiles specify PyTorch 2.11.0/CUDA 13.0; π0.5 uses ten warm-ups and 50 timed iterations. Appendix A separately specifies A40, PhyAI 0.1.0, Python 3.12.11 and MuJoCo 3.2.3.

RoboTwin requires matching q01/q99 normalization and swapping wrist views into head/left/right order. Appendix B describes 100 episodes but supplies no success number or exact archived revision. Appendix C omits its GPU model; Appendix A mentions a pinned image without printing its digest.

Appendix D specifies eight H20 workers, 32 clients, local graph batch four, padding and up-to-20-ms batch formation, using one-action chunks. It supplies no aggregate throughput or success. A reproduction must measure full request wait as well as compute time.

reasoning.text: The technical-resource placement and architecture/prediction/quadrant 'Not applicable' fit an inference infrastructure paper supporting heterogeneous policies. Shared runtime code does not establish a One Model WAM. The training-optimization tag applies indirectly through rollout acceleration; PhyAI proposes no distillation method.

discussionQuestions: Can exact cache reuse and graph replay preserve episode outcomes under changing observations and partial batches?
How much of the projected RL gain survives backend synchronization and queueing?

evidence.location: PDF p. 1, title, author block and arXiv margin
evidence.detail: The title and all 26 authors match the catalog; the PDF is arXiv:2608.03682v3, dated 14 August 2026. Six institutional affiliations are printed.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 2–3, Section 1; p. 4, Section 2.2
evidence.detail: PhyAI shares an inference path across deployment settings while leaving training and RL orchestration to existing systems.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 5–6, Section 3.1, Equations (1)–(2)
evidence.detail: Camera observations, instruction and robot state produce an action chunk. Observation-to-handoff latency includes observation, transfer, queueing, inference and actuation, but excludes execution of the returned actions.

evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Section 3.2, Equations (3)–(8); p. 7, Figure 2 and Sections 3.3–3.4
evidence.detail: Sequential control adds inference and environment time; ideal overlap takes their maximum. The plotted timing omits other request overheads. Figure 2 shows four LIBERO-suite comparisons on RTX PRO 6000 and a separate AGX Orin star.

evidence.location: PDF p. 7, Section 3.4, Equation (9)
evidence.detail: Throughput is batch size divided by synchronized batch time; amortized per-sample time is not the wait experienced by a request.

evidence.location: PDF p. 8, Sections 4–4.2 and Figure 3
evidence.detail: Adapters define policy semantics; the scheduler places requests; runners own buffers, caches and graph buckets; stateless modeling modules call shared Layers and shape-dependent kernel dispatch.

evidence.location: PDF p. 9, Section 4.2, Kernel fusion, Graph replay, Profiled operator selection and Quantization
evidence.detail: The π0.5 prefix is reused within ten Euler steps and invalidated for new conditions. Fixed timestep/modulation tables and graph capture reduce repeated work. Offline round-to-nearest quantization is separate from BF16 batch profiles.

evidence.location: PDF p. 9, Section 4.2, Kernel fusion, MiniCPM-Robot paragraph
evidence.detail: On H20 in BF16, adding two fused kernels to the CUDA Graph path changes throughput from 33.28 to 36.77 Hz, a reported 10.5% gain; kernels are checked against FP32/BF16 PyTorch references.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 9–10, Section 4.3, Figure 4 and Equation (10)
evidence.detail: Independent π0.5 requests use DP. Cosmos3 jointly evolves video/action tokens using TP within conditional and unconditional branches, matching-rank CFG all-gather, rank-local guidance and UniPC. Video VAE decoding is optional after the final step.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 10–11, Section 5.1, Table 4 and Equations (11)–(13)
evidence.detail: Measurements concern model-runner action-chunk time. Phase/batch profiles use BF16; logical tensor traffic is modeled rather than measured DRAM traffic. Profiles use PyTorch 2.11.0 and CUDA 13.0; the Hopper-series GPU model is not specified.

evidence.location: PDF p. 11, Section 5.2 and Table 5, all model/device rows; p. 1, Figure 1
evidence.detail: All 11 official-to-PhyAI pairs in Table 5 improve by 1.40×–4.65×. Cosmos3 on eight H20 GPUs takes 2460 versus 1180 ms with CFG degree two and TP degree four. Specialized runtimes can be faster and available comparisons are not fully precision matched.

evidence.location: PDF p. 12, Section 5.3, PI0.5 paragraph and Figure 5
evidence.detail: BF16 π0.5 with three views, 50 actions, ten Euler steps and CUDA Graphs uses ten warm-ups and 50 timed iterations. Hopper throughput rises from 44.26 to 100.02 samples/s between batches one and 32, while full-batch time rises from 22.59 to 319.94 ms. Thor batch four is explicitly noisy.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 12–13, Section 5.3, GR00T paragraph and Figure 6
evidence.detail: RTX 5090 GR00T BF16 throughput rises from 48.8 to 138.8 samples/s from batch one to 32; batch eight reaches 92.2% of batch-32 throughput. Backbone overtakes Action Head from batch four. The figure includes runner-latency P99 measurements.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 12–13, Section 5.3, Cosmos3 paragraph and Figure 7; p. 10, Table 4
evidence.detail: The eager BF16 sweep uses four denoising steps, guidance scale 3.0, 32 actions at 15 Hz and 33 frames at 480 × 832, excluding optional video decode. Hopper throughput rises from 0.883 to 1.010 chunks/s as batch grows one to 16; full-batch time reaches 15.85 s. RTX 5090 runs out of memory.

evidence.location: PDF p. 14, Figure 8 and Section 5.3 analysis; p. 11, Section 5.1
evidence.detail: At batch one the Hopper π0.5 expert has 8.8% of estimated FLOPs but 57.2% of profiled time; at batch 32 its time share is 13.5%. Cosmos3 generation is compute-heavy in the measured logical-intensity diagnostic, which does not establish TP/CFG scaling.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 14–16, Section 5.4; p. 15, Table 6 and Figure 9
evidence.detail: A four-A800-80-GB GRPO LIBERO-10 baseline step takes 955.8 s, with maximum-rank predict time 152.4 s. A measured 2.55× mean-predict speedup motivates an idealized 863.2 s step projection; the 1.11× end-to-end speedup is not measured.

evidence.location: PDF p. 3, Section 1, simulated RL rollout paragraph; p. 16, Section 6.3
evidence.detail: The introduction separately reports an eight-A100 simulation with batch 40 and 41 policy calls per RL step, estimating 26.5% lower step latency and about 1.36× throughput. Section 6.3 still describes usable RLinf backend integration as future work.

evidence.location: PDF p. 16, Sections 5.5 and 6.1–6.4; p. 17, Sections 6.5–7.3
evidence.detail: The main evaluation summary limits runtime claims and excludes full deployment overheads. Persistent kernels, kernel-agent tuning, broader support and a production serving protocol are future work. Hardware-cost and control-budget trades are proposed rather than quantified.

evidence.location: PDF p. 22, Appendix A, Inference server, Evaluation protocol, Results and Table 7
evidence.detail: GR00T-N1.7-LIBERO/libero_10 is evaluated on A40 with two 256 × 256 views, batch one, first eight actions executed, 720-step cap, 50 initial states per task and seeds 42–91. Matched official/PhyAI trials yield 456/500 (91.2%) versus 459/500 (91.8%).

evidence.location: PDF pp. 22–23, Appendix B and Table 8
evidence.detail: RoboTwin requires the motus-robotics/pi0.5_robotwin2 checkpoint, matched q01/q99 normalization, reordered head/left/right views, BF16, ten denoising steps and 32 × 14 outputs; ten actions are executed at 30 Hz. A 100-episode evaluation is described without a numerical success result.

evidence.location: PDF p. 23, Appendix C, Model configuration, Simulation protocol, Results and Table 9
evidence.detail: Four LIBERO suites each use 500 episodes, synchronous ten-action chunks, BF16, FlashInfer and CUDA Graphs. Success counts are 489, 499, 490 and 471, totaling 1949/2000; mean inference ranges 36.10–36.33 ms. No matched baseline or GPU model is listed here.

evidence.location: PDF p. 24, Appendix D and Table 10
evidence.detail: An eight-H20 demonstration serves 32 clients with maximum server batch 32, local graph batch four, up-to-20-ms batching wait and one-action chunks. Padding handles incomplete batches; no aggregate throughput or success result is supplied.

evidence.location: PDF p. 25, Appendix E and Table 11
evidence.detail: BF16 π0 evaluates spatial and object suites with 100 episodes each, batch one and 50-action chunks exhausted before replanning. Results are 71/100 and 72/100, totaling 143/200 (71.5%), without a matched runtime baseline.
